key_terms.meaning: A conduction electron in a metal is treated as moving freely between ions, with a random thermal speed of about 10⁶ m/s and no net velocity when no field is applied.
The average time τ between two scattering events; after a collision the electron loses its directed drift and starts again.
The small extra velocity v_d = eEτ/m (order 10⁻⁴ m/s) that the field E adds on top of the random motion.
σ = ne²τ/m, with n the electron density in m⁻³, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, τ in seconds and m = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
Quantised lattice vibrations; at room temperature they are the main thing an electron collides with, so τ falls as T rises.
Foreign atoms, vacancies and grain boundaries; they scatter electrons and set a temperature-independent floor on resistivity.
σ/(κT) is nearly the same constant for all metals, because the same electrons carry both charge and heat.
The energy of the highest filled state at 0 K; in a metal it is a few electron volts (about 7 eV for copper).
g(E), the number of allowed states per unit energy per unit volume; for a 3D free electron gas g(E) ∝ √E.
m* is the mass that makes an electron in a band respond to a force as if it were free; it can differ greatly from m and can even be negative (a hole).
The energy range with no allowed states between the valence band and the conduction band; E_g = 1.1 eV for silicon.
A pure crystal where every conduction electron comes from breaking a bond, so n = p = n_i.
A crystal with donor or acceptor atoms added; a donor gives an electron (n-type), an acceptor gives a hole (p-type).

key_terms.term: Fermi level in a doped semiconductor
key_terms.meaning: E_F sits just below the conduction band in n-type and just above the valence band in p-type, and moves to mid-gap as T rises.
μ = v_d/E, in m²/(V·s); the drift velocity per unit field, limited by scattering.
D/μ = k_BT/e, linking the diffusion constant D (m²/s) to the mobility at temperature T.
The potential step at a metal–semiconductor contact, roughly φ_B = φ_m − χ for n-type; it rectifies the current.
A region, typically micrometres across, in which atomic moments in a ferromagnet are already aligned without any applied field.
The reverse field needed to bring B back to zero; the loop area is the energy lost per unit volume per magnetisation cycle.

takeaways: Treating electrons as a classical gas gives Ohm's law, σ = ne²τ/m, and the right order of magnitude for metal conductivity, but it cannot explain the tiny electronic heat capacity.
Quantum statistics fix this: only electrons within about k_BT of the Fermi energy can be excited, so the classical value is multiplied by the small ratio T/T_F.
The periodic lattice turns a continuous free-electron parabola into bands separated by gaps, and the gap size decides metal, semiconductor or insulator.
Doping pins the majority carrier density at the dopant level; mass action law np = n_i² then fixes the minority carriers and the Fermi level.
Total current in a semiconductor is drift plus diffusion, and the Einstein relation lets you keep only one of μ or D in the equations.
A metal–semiconductor contact is ohmic when the barrier is negligible or thin enough to tunnel, and rectifying when a stable Schottky barrier forms.
Diamagnets oppose the field weakly, paramagnets follow it weakly, and ferromagnets align in domains and can stay magnetised after the field is removed.
The area of the B–H loop is the energy lost as heat per cycle, so transformers use narrow-loop soft magnets and loudspeakers use wide-loop hard magnets.
bank_note: Long answers here almost always ask for a derivation plus a failure list — the Drude derivation and its comparison with the quantum picture, or a carrier-concentration derivation with the temperature regimes.

bank.q: State the assumptions of the classical free electron theory of metals and derive the expression σ = ne²τ/m for electrical conductivity.
outline: Define n, e, m, τ and v_d and state each assumption: free, independent, random motion, collisions only
Write the equation of motion m dv_d/dt = eE − m v_d/τ and solve for steady state
Get v_d = eEτ/m, then J = nev_d = (ne²τ/m)E
Identify σ = ne²τ/m and check units (S/m)
Use the Drude model to predict ρ and compare with the measured value for a metal

bank.q: Explain the Fermi–Dirac distribution function and show why only a small fraction of conduction electrons take part in conduction.
outline: Write f(E) with E_F and k_BT defined and draw it at 0 K and at 300 K
State that f(E_F) = 1/2 at any T > 0
Show the fraction of participating electrons is of order T/T_F
Explain how this removes the heat capacity contradiction
Note T_F is of order 10⁴–10⁵ K for typical metals

bank.q: Distinguish between intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors with respect to band gap, carrier density, Fermi level and temperature dependence.
outline: Intrinsic: n = p = n_i, E_F near mid-gap, strong rise of n_i with T
Extrinsic: n ≈ N_D or p ≈ N_A at room temperature, E_F near a band edge
Three temperature regimes: freeze-out, saturation, intrinsic
Mass action law np = n_i²
Two numerical values of E_g, for example silicon 1.1 eV and germanium 0.7 eV

bank.q: Derive the density of states for a free electron gas in three dimensions and explain the meaning of effective mass.
outline: Count states inside a sphere of radius k in k-space with periodic boundary conditions
Convert to energy using E = ħ²k²/2m
Obtain g(E) ∝ √E and state the constant
Explain why a band electron uses m* instead of m
Mention that m* comes from d²E/dk² and is negative near the top of a band, which is described as a hole

bank.q: A silicon sample is doped with 10²² m⁻³ donor atoms and has n_i = 1.5 × 10¹⁶ m⁻³ at 300 K. Find the hole density, the Fermi level position and the conductivity, taking μ_e = 0.13 m²/(V·s).
outline: Assume full ionisation so n ≈ N_D
Apply np = n_i² to get p = n_i²/N_D ≈ 2.25 × 10¹⁰ m⁻³
Use n = N_C exp[−(E_C − E_F)/k_BT] to find E_C − E_F
Compute σ = neμ_e with n = 10²² m⁻³ and e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C
State the units and comment on why the hole contribution is neglected

bank.q: Starting from the drift and diffusion current densities, derive the Einstein relation D/μ = k_BT/e.
outline: Write J_n = neμ_nE + eD_n dn/dx
Set J_n = 0 at equilibrium
Use the Boltzmann expression n = n_0 exp(eV/k_BT) with E = −dV/dx
Cancel terms to obtain D_n/μ_n = k_BT/e
Give the same result for holes and a typical value of D at 300 K

bank.q: Explain the formation of a Schottky barrier at a metal–n-type semiconductor contact and describe two ways to make the contact ohmic.
outline: Draw the band diagram before and after contact, showing charge transfer and band bending
Define barrier height φ_B = φ_m − χ and built-in potential
State the rectifying condition φ_m > φ_s
Method 1: choose a metal with low work function so φ_m < φ_s
Method 2: dope the semiconductor heavily so the barrier is thin and carriers tunnel

bank.q: Compare the classical and quantum free electron theories of metals, and show clearly which experimental facts each one explains and which it fails to explain.
outline: Successes of the classical theory: Ohm's law, order of magnitude of σ, Wiedemann–Franz ratio
Failure: electronic heat capacity comes out about 100 times too large
Failure: it cannot separate metals from insulators and predicts the wrong speed dependence
Quantum theory: Fermi–Dirac statistics, only T/T_F electrons active, correct heat capacity
Quantum theory keeps the Wiedemann–Franz law and explains why σ is large
Conclude that the classical theory survives only as a first estimate of σ

bank.q: Sketch and explain the B–H hysteresis loop of a ferromagnet. Discuss why soft magnets are used in transformer cores and hard magnets in permanent magnets.
outline: Label saturation, retentivity, coercivity and the loop area
Explain the loop through domain wall motion and domain rotation
State that loop area = energy lost per unit volume per cycle
Soft magnet: narrow loop, low coercivity, low loss, high permeability
Hard magnet: wide loop, high coercivity, large retentivity, stores energy
Name one application of each (transformer core, loudspeaker or motor magnet)

bank.q: Discuss the temperature dependence of electrical conductivity in a metal and in an extrinsic semiconductor, and explain the physics of each region.
outline: Metal: σ falls as T rises because phonon scattering reduces τ
Metal: Matthiessen's rule, residual resistivity from impurities at low T
Semiconductor: freeze-out region, saturation region, intrinsic region
In the saturation region n is fixed by doping but μ still falls with T
In the intrinsic region n_i rises exponentially and dominates
Plot log σ against 1/T and mark the three regions

bank.q: Explain why an ohmic contact is essential in a semiconductor device, and evaluate the practical difficulty of making one to a lightly doped semiconductor.
outline: Define an ohmic contact: linear I–V, negligible contact resistance, no rectification
Explain what goes wrong if a Schottky contact forms at a device terminal
Barrier height depends on work function difference and on surface states
Heavy doping is the usual practical route because it gives a thin tunnelling barrier
Mention that contact resistance adds to series resistance and wastes power
Conclude with the trade-off between doping level and device behaviour

bank.q: Compare the magnetic behaviour of diamagnetic, paramagnetic and ferromagnetic materials, giving the sign and size of susceptibility, the origin of the moment and one application of each.
outline: Diamagnetism: induced opposing moment, small negative χ, present in all materials
Paramagnetism: permanent atomic moments, χ positive and of order 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻³, Curie law
Ferromagnetism: exchange interaction aligns moments in domains, χ large and non-linear
Curie temperature and loss of ferromagnetism above it
Hysteresis and remanence exist only in ferromagnets
One application each: superconductors or bismuth, oxygen sensors or MRI contrast, transformer cores

bank.q: Explain the origin of energy bands in a solid, using the nearly free electron picture and the qualitative Kronig–Penney result, and use it to separate metals, semiconductors and insulators.
outline: Start from free electrons and add a weak periodic potential
State Bloch's theorem: ψ = u(x)e^{ikx} with u periodic
Show that gaps open where the Bragg condition k = ±π/a is satisfied
Sketch the E–k diagram and the reduced zone scheme
Metal: partly filled band; semiconductor: small gap with thermal excitation; insulator: large gap
Quote E_g values and state the E_g is the only criterion at fixed temperature

glossary.def: The classical model of a metal as a gas of independent electrons that accelerate in a field and lose their drift at each collision.
The average distance an electron travels between collisions, equal to v_th τ, typically a few tens of nanometres in a metal at room temperature.
The surface in k-space at 0 K that contains all the filled electron states, with radius k_F.
T_F = E_F/k_B, of order 10⁴–10⁵ K in metals; it is not a real temperature of the electrons.
An electron gas in which k_BT is much smaller than E_F, so quantum statistics matter and the classical equipartition result fails.
In a periodic potential the wavefunction has the form ψ(x) = u(x)e^{ikx}, where u has the period of the lattice.
A one-dimensional lattice of rectangular potential wells, solved to show how allowed bands and forbidden gaps appear.
A way of drawing E–k that folds all bands into the first Brillouin zone, −π/a ≤ k ≤ π/a.
A missing electron in an almost full band, which behaves as a positive charge with its own effective mass.
An impurity atom, such as phosphorus in silicon, that gives up an electron to the conduction band and makes the crystal n-type.
An impurity atom, such as boron in silicon, that accepts an electron and leaves a hole, making the crystal p-type.
At thermal equilibrium np = n_i², whatever the doping level.
The small energy (about 0.01–0.05 eV) needed to free a donor electron or to free a hole from an acceptor.
Part of a semiconductor away from junctions where the space charge is negligible and n − p equals the fixed ion charge.
Current caused by carriers moving from high to low concentration, J_n = eD_n dn/dx.
The energy needed to remove an electron from a metal to vacuum, written φ_m and measured in electron volts.
The energy released when an electron drops from vacuum into the bottom of a semiconductor's conduction band, written χ.
The equilibrium band bending at a junction, written V_bi, that balances diffusion and drift.
A contact so heavily doped that the barrier is thin and carriers cross by quantum tunnelling, giving a nearly linear I–V curve.
μ = μ_r μ_0, the constant that relates B to H in a material; μ_0 = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m.
χ = M/H, the ratio of magnetisation to applied field; it is small and negative for diamagnets and large and positive for ferromagnets.
The temperature above which a ferromagnet loses its spontaneous magnetisation and becomes paramagnetic; about 770 °C for iron.
The flux density left in a material when the applied field is reduced to zero after saturation.
The largest value of B×H around the demagnetisation curve; it measures how good a permanent magnet is.
